title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 32
paragraphs: Seven days had gone by since Prince Andrew had found himself at the dressing station on the field of Borodino. In the doctor's opinion, his fever and the inflammation of his injured bowels were sure to kill him. But on the seventh day he ate a piece of bread with tea and enjoyed it, and the doctor saw that his temperature was lower. He had come to his senses that morning. The first night after they left Moscow had been fairly warm, so he had stayed in the calèche. At Mytishchi, though, the wounded man himself asked to be taken out and given some tea. Being carried into the hut hurt so much that he groaned aloud and lost consciousness again. Once they had laid him on his camp bed, he lay motionless with his eyes shut for a long time. Then he opened them and whispered: "And the tea?" The doctor was astonished that he remembered such a small detail of daily life. He felt Prince Andrew's pulse and found, to his surprise and annoyance, that it was better. He was annoyed because experience had taught him that if the patient did not die now, he would die a little later and suffer more. Timokhin, the red-nosed major of Prince Andrew's regiment, had joined him in Moscow and was being taken along with him, wounded in the leg at Borodino. With them traveled a doctor, Prince Andrew's valet, his coachman and two orderlies.
They gave Prince Andrew some tea. He drank it eagerly, his feverish eyes fixed on the door in front of him, as if he were trying to understand and remember something.
"I don't want any more. Is Timokhin here?" he asked.
Timokhin crawled along the bench toward him.
"I'm here, your excellency."
"How is your wound?"
"Mine, sir? It's all right. But how are you?"
Prince Andrew again grew thoughtful, as if trying to remember something.
"Could someone find me a book?" he asked.
"What book?"
"The Gospels. I don't have one."

The doctor promised to get it for him and began asking how he felt. Prince Andrew answered every question reluctantly but sensibly. Then he said he wanted a bolster under him, because he was uncomfortable and in great pain. The doctor and the valet lifted the cloak that covered him. They made faces at the foul smell of rotting flesh from the wound and began examining that dreadful place. Something displeased the doctor very much, and he changed the dressings. He turned the wounded man over, and Prince Andrew groaned again, and the agony made him lose consciousness and rave. He kept asking them to get him the book and put it under him.
"What trouble would it be for you?" he said. "I don't have one. Please get it and put it under me for a moment," he begged in a pitiful voice.
The doctor went out into the passage to wash his hands.
"You fellows have no conscience," he said to the valet, who was pouring water over his hands. "I took my eyes off you for one moment... The pain is so bad, you know, that I wonder how he bears it."
"By the Lord Jesus Christ, I thought we'd put something under him!" said the valet.

The first time Prince Andrew understood where he was and what was wrong with him, and remembered that he was wounded and how, was when he asked to be carried into the hut after his calèche stopped at Mytishchi. Pain had confused him while he was carried in, but he came to again. While he drank his tea he recalled everything that had happened to him. Above all he remembered vividly the moment at the dressing station when, seeing the suffering of a man he disliked, those new thoughts had come to him that promised him happiness. Those thoughts, though vague and indistinct now, took hold of his soul again. He remembered that he now had a new source of happiness, and that this happiness had something to do with the Gospels. That was why he had asked for a copy. But the awkward position they had put him in, and the turning over, had muddled his thoughts again. When he came to himself a third time, it was in the complete stillness of the night. Everyone near him was asleep. A cricket chirped across the passage, and someone in the street was shouting and singing. Cockroaches rustled on the table, on the icons and on the walls. A big fly flopped about at the head of the bed and around the candle beside him, whose charred wick had curled into the shape of a mushroom.

His mind was not in a normal state. A healthy man usually thinks of, feels and remembers countless things at once. Yet he has the power and the will to pick one train of thoughts or events and fix his whole attention on it. A healthy man can tear himself away from his deepest reflections to say a polite word to someone who comes in, and then go back to his own thoughts. In that respect Prince Andrew's mind was not normal. All its powers were more active and clearer than ever, but they worked apart from his will. The most varied thoughts and images filled his mind at the same time. At moments his brain suddenly worked with a vigor, clarity and depth it had never reached when he was well. Then, in the middle of that work, it would veer off to some unexpected idea, and he had no strength to turn it back.

"Yes, a new happiness was revealed to me, one that man cannot be deprived of," he thought, as he lay in the half-darkness of the quiet hut, staring ahead with wide, feverish eyes. "A happiness that lies beyond material forces, outside the material influences that act on a man — a happiness of the soul alone, the happiness of loving. Every man can understand it, but only God could conceive it and command it. But how did God command that law? And why was the Son...?"

And suddenly this train of thought broke off. Prince Andrew heard (without knowing whether it was delusion or reality) a soft whispering voice repeating over and over, in a steady rhythm, "piti-piti-piti," then "titi," and then "piti-piti-piti" again, and "ti-ti" once more. At the same time he felt that above his face, right over its middle, some strange airy structure of slender needles or splinters was being built, to the sound of this whispered music. He felt he had to balance carefully (though it was hard) to keep this airy structure from collapsing. Yet it kept collapsing and slowly rising again to the sound of the whispered rhythmic music. "It stretches, stretches, spreading out and stretching," Prince Andrew said to himself. As he listened to the whispering and felt this drawing out and the building of the edifice of needles, he also saw, in glimpses, a red halo around the candle. He heard the rustle of the cockroaches and the buzzing of the fly that flopped against his pillow and his face. Each time the fly touched his face it burned him, and yet, to his surprise, it did not destroy the structure, though it struck the very spot on his face where the structure was rising. But there was something else of importance too. It was something white by the door — the statue of a sphinx, which also weighed on him.

"But perhaps that's my shirt on the table," he thought, "and that's my legs, and that's the door. But why does it keep stretching and drawing itself out, and 'piti-piti-piti' and 'ti-ti' and 'piti-piti-piti'...? That's enough, please stop!" Prince Andrew begged someone in anguish. And suddenly thoughts and feelings rose again to the surface of his mind with remarkable clarity and force.

"Yes — love," he thought again, quite clearly. "But not the love that loves for something, for some quality, some purpose or some reason. It's the love I first felt, while dying, when I saw my enemy and still loved him. I felt that love which is the very essence of the soul and needs no object. Now I feel that bliss again. To love your neighbors, to love your enemies, to love everything, to love God in all His forms. You can love someone dear to you with human love, but an enemy can be loved only with divine love. That is why I felt such joy when I realized that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?...

"When you love with human love, you can pass from love to hatred, but divine love cannot change. No, neither death nor anything else can destroy it. It is the very essence of the soul. And yet how many people I have hated in my life! Of them all, there was none I loved and hated as I did her." And he pictured Natasha vividly. He no longer saw only her charms, which had delighted him before. For the first time he pictured her soul. And he understood her feelings, her suffering, her shame and remorse. For the first time he understood how cruel it had been to reject her, how cruel his break with her. "If only I could see her once more! Just once, to look into those eyes and say..."

"Piti-piti-piti and ti-ti and piti-piti-piti boom!" the fly flopped.... And his attention was suddenly carried into another world, a world of reality and delirium in which something peculiar was happening. In that world some structure was still going up and had not fallen, something was still stretching out, and the candle with its red halo was still burning, and the same shirtlike sphinx lay by the door. But besides all this, something creaked, a breath of fresh air came in, and a new white sphinx appeared, standing at the door. And that sphinx had the pale face and shining eyes of the very Natasha he had just been thinking about.

"Oh, how oppressive this endless delirium is," thought Prince Andrew, trying to drive that face out of his imagination. But the face stayed in front of him with the force of reality and came nearer. Prince Andrew wanted to return to that earlier world of pure thought, but he couldn't, and the delirium drew him back into its realm. The soft whispering voice went on with its rhythmic murmur, something weighed on him and stretched out, and the strange face was in front of him. Prince Andrew gathered all his strength to recover his senses. He moved a little, and suddenly his ears rang, his eyes dimmed, and like a man plunged into water he lost consciousness. When he came to himself, Natasha was kneeling in front of him — that same living Natasha whom, of all people, he most longed to love with this new, pure, divine love that had been revealed to him. He realized that it was the real, living Natasha, and he was not surprised but quietly happy. Natasha knelt motionless (she could not stir), her frightened eyes fixed on him, holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and rigid. Only in its lower part did something quiver.
Prince Andrew sighed with relief, smiled and held out his hand.
"You?" he said. "How fortunate!"
Quickly but carefully, Natasha moved closer to him on her knees. She took his hand gently, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.
"Forgive me!" she whispered, raising her head and glancing at him. "Forgive me!"
"I love you," said Prince Andrew.
"Forgive...!"
"Forgive what?" he asked.
"Forgive me for what I ha-ve do-ne!" Natasha faltered in a broken, scarcely audible whisper, and she kissed his hand faster, just touching it with her lips.
"I love you more, and better, than before," said Prince Andrew, lifting her face with his hand so that he could look into her eyes.

Those eyes, full of happy tears, looked at him timidly, with compassion and joyful love. Natasha's thin, pale face, with its swollen lips, was more than plain — it was dreadful. But Prince Andrew didn't see that. He saw her shining eyes, which were beautiful. Behind them they heard voices.

Peter the valet, now wide awake, had roused the doctor. Timokhin had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg. He had been watching everything for a long time, huddled on his bench and carefully covering his bare body with the sheet.
"What's this?" said the doctor, getting up from his bed. "Please go away, madam!"
At that moment a maid knocked at the door. The countess had sent her, having noticed that her daughter was missing.
Like a sleepwalker woken from her sleep, Natasha left the room. She went back to her hut and fell sobbing on her bed.

From then on, for the whole rest of the Rostovs' journey, at every halt and wherever they spent the night, Natasha never left the wounded Bolkonski. The doctor had to admit that he had not expected such firmness or such skill in nursing a wounded man from a young girl.

The countess imagined how dreadful it would be if Prince Andrew died in her daughter's arms during the journey — and, judging by what the doctor said, that might easily happen — but she could not oppose Natasha. A closeness had now grown up between the wounded man and Natasha, and it crossed her mind that if he recovered, their former engagement would be renewed. Still, no one spoke of this, least of all Natasha and Prince Andrew. The unsettled question of life and death, which hung not only over Bolkonski but over all Russia, shut out every other consideration.
